content.title: Some clarification
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the feedback. We would like to address a few points:  

- *"This paper seems to be a mixture of existing techniques. Tuning soft prompts is proposed and discussed in Li and Liang 2021 and Lester et. al. 2021. Using entities for improving and controlling summarization is previously discussed in many works, for example Sharma et. al. 2019. Combining these techniques seems to be more of an engineering effort than scientific contribution."*   
-> We are the first to show that combining soft prompts with entities guidance can achieve a triple goal of parameter-efficiency, high few-shot performance and controllability. Simply combining these two techniques won't work well (Table 4: Promptsumm no-pretraining). We design a unique 2nd pretraining stage (Sec 3.3) to make it work.

- *"The authors claim that their approach is parameter and data efficient. Yet this paper uses C4 to pretrain the language model, which is neither parameter nor data efficient. Although the following fine-tune stage only tunes the prompt, it would be improper to turn a blind eye on the pretraining stage."*   
-> We'd like to clarify that "parameter and data efficient" refers to the fine-tuning stage, not the pre-training stage as the reviewer pointed. We will make this claim clear in next version. Upon acceptance, we will release our pre-trained models and soft prompts, which enables users fine-tuning a controllable, parameter-efficient and data efficient summarizer for any downstream datasets.

- *"Yet in Table 2, it would be very hard to compare models due to multiple changing factors: the number of tunable parameters are not the same; the base model is not the same; this work has additional pretraining while others may not; this work uses explicit entity models while others have not. Given these facts, unless I have missed something, it would be very hard to conclude that this work is truly parameter-efficient or data-efficient."*   
-> We would like to clarify that the goal of Table 2 is to compare the performance of published literature on few-shot summarization, not to provide an ablation. 

- *"Table 4 is very hard to parse. I can make an educated guess yet feel like refrained to do so. It would be great if the authors could clearly state what are the differences between models (e.g., what are the differences between Soft PT v.s. PromptSum?)."*   
-> Table 4 shows a model ablation. The difference between Soft PT and PromptSum is that Soft PT does not use any input entity chain.

content.title: Prefix-Tuning comparison
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the feedback.  

*"Compared to the baseline model, the prefix tuning method gets strong results in the original prefixtuning paper, Li and Liang, 2021. PEGASUS was used by the authors here, but their results, even in zero and one shot, were much worse. "*   
-> Prefix-tuning only showed the performance on XSum, dataset on the which our model is outperforming Prefix-Tuning 0.1% (but not Prefix-Tuning 2.0%, although we are reasonably close). Besides, Prefix-tuning uses BART as backbone LM, while we use PEGASUS, which is stronger than BART for few-shot abstractive summarization, especially on XSum 100-shot.

content.title: Some clarification
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the feedback.
We wish to clarify a few points:
- Weakness 1:  
*"It is important to note that the costs of forward passes during training and inference are still present."*   
-> Prompt tuning is emerging and promising in the era of large pre-trained language models. Instead of fine-tuning a large model for each downstream task, one can just learn a very lightweight prompt for each task while keeping the backbone PLM frozen. Though computation costs during inference is still present like reviewer mentioned, the memory cost and hardware requirement during training is considerably reduced.  
*"It is not clear if the fine-tuning stage described in Section 3.3 will generate two separate PEGASUS checkpoints."*   
-> We would like to point out that the fine-tuning process of PromptSum only generates two soft prompts, and not two entire model checkpoints. Therefore, it is a very light-weight fine-tuning. However, as the reviewer points out, due to the double inference, the FLOPS is indeed multiplied by 2. 
- Minor comment 1:  
[P_E, X_i] is indeed a concatenation operation. 
- Minor comment 2:  
We thank the reviewer for pointing out this inconsistency that the concatenation should be written [X_i, P_E]. When both prompts are used, the order is [X_i, P_S, E]. 
- Minor comment 3:   
We used 8 GPUs for pre-training.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper develops a parameter efficient training for discrete prompt based summarization. The paper uses PEGASUS backbone with discrete entity guided prompts  and summarization objectives for finetuning. It uses sequence of entities (or entity chains) as a high level plans to bootstrap the generation prices.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Pros:
 
- Paper is very well written and easy to follow.
- Ablations are informative and relevant.
- Entity chains as prompts is a very intuitive and simple idea. Ablations show the value of using these in summarization process is promising. These entity chains are also human interpretable and this adds value. 
 
Cons:
 
- Evaluation remains one of the main drawbacks. It is not surprising that Promptsum does better on XSum (since the summaries are short and additional entities as prompts is expected to improve the summaries by addressing the hallucination issues discussed in the paper). The entities not achieving better performance (than baselines) on other dataset with longer summaries shows that the approach might not be useful for other summarization tasks that contain longer summaries. In other words, entity chains as prompts don't add new  information than those already learnt by the models trained with summarization objective. One interesting evaluation would be to evaluate if human generated prompts generate better summaries.
- ROUGE scores as metrics have been shown to not be very reliant for summarization evaluation. Reporting other metrics (human & automatic evaluations could generate more insights about the model summaries)
- Human evaluations (Table 8) needs more statistical tests. It's difficult to parse if the difference are significant. For instance, one would expect factualness to improve with entity chains, but human evaluation doesn't show major differences indicating that the prompts aren't improving the factualness.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The contributions of the paper are clear with multi-task mixture of prompts summary generation.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper uses parameter efficient prompt tuning methods with soft and discrete prompts. It creates a multi-objective learning setup with entity link generations. The model achieves state-of-the-art results on several popular few-shot benchmarks as well as a strong level of controllability through entities, all while only tuning several orders of magnitude less parameters.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper addresses the problem of parameter-efficient tuning of large language models to specific tasks via Prompt Tuning (PT). The authors propose a mixture-of-prompts technique that leverages soft prompts (Lester et al., 2021) that are learned via backprogagation and discrete prompts (entity chains, Liu & Chen, 2021) that provide a content plan to the generation task. Their PromptSum framework comprises two subtasks: (1) generation of discrete entities E from an input text X; (2) generation of a output Y conditioned on both X and E. They conduct text summarization experiments using four benchmarks (CNN/DM, XSum, BillSum, and SAMSum) covering diverse domains. They claim to achieve state-of-the-art results in few-shot summarization as measured by ROUGE, as well as "impressive levels of controlability" of summaries even with few-shot supervision.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
1. The paper is well motivated and tackles a relevant problem of efficient domain adaptation using large language models.
2. Authors provide extensive summarization experiments on diverse domains.
3. Good description of hyperparameter settings that contribute to reproducibility.
4. Good controllability results, at the expense of summarization performance (see weakness 2 below).

Weaknesses:
1.  Overstatement of parameter efficiency: in Section 4.2, the authors state that "Despite containing three order of magnitude less parameters than the former type of models." The authors should be careful in stating that this parameter efficiency refers to the optimization of a limited set of parameters during training and fine-tuning. It is important to note that the costs of forward passes during training and inference are still present. Furthermore, the two-step inference procedure (the first being discrete entity generation) is at least two times more expensive than the original PEGASUS in terms of FLOPS. It is not clear if the fine-tuning stage described in Section 3.3 will generate two separate PEGASUS checkpoints. If that is the case, PromptSum would also be more costly in terms of memory. These trade-offs deserve more discussion in the paper.
2.  Overstatement of results: while the authors claim to achieve "state-of-the-art few-shot ROUGE summarization results" in the introduction, the actual results on most tasks are underwhelming. Note that PromptSum weights are initialized from "google/pegasus-large" (HuggingFace checkpoint) so the baseline performance for the model is PEGASUS, making the comparison to the other baselines not informative or irrelevant. Also, the results show that their method actually hurts the performance of pretrained PEGASUS in most settings. A similar trend is observed in Table 4, which shows that "Soft PT" consistently outperforms PromptSum. For XSum, the summarization results seem promising but unfortunately, the authors fail to investigate or discuss what is special about the XSum dataset that makes PromptSum apparently well suited to this task.
3.  Method limitations: each soft prompt uses 300 tokens out of the 1024 maximum input length of PEGASUS (and even more tokens if combined with entity chains, for which the lengths are not specified). This represents a serious limitation for the applicability of this model. Why this number of tokens is needed when Lester et al. (2021) achieve good results with 20 tokens?
4.  Potential inconsistency in results: the reviewer could not find the reported XSum results for PSP (32.50 R1 in Table 2) in the Liu et al. (2022) publication. How were those results obtained? And since PSP is also trained on CNN/DM, why not include it as a baseline for CNN/DM?

Minor comments:
1. In Equation 1, is the operator [P_E, X_i] a concatenation? If so, it should be clearly stated and maybe the use of [P_E; X_i] would be more appropriate to agree with the notation of Lester et al. (2021).
2. Still in Equation 1, you should use [X_i; P_E] to agree with your experimental setup in Section 4.1: "We concatenate each soft prompt to the right of the source document". When you have both P_S and E, what is the concatenation order? (Figure 1 suggests [X, P_S, E] while Equation 2 shows [P_S, X, E]).
3. Vague statements:
	- "We pre-train for 400k steps, using an effective batch size of 256 and data parallelism over multiple GPUs": why not specify the number of GPUs?
	- "PromptSum achieves several state-of-the-art results on XSum few-shot, and wildly outperforms the comparable parameter-efficient PSP on XSum."
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The proposed mix-of-prompts method adds novelty and is presented in a clear way overall. It has some notation issues and vagueness of language that needs to be addressed (see "minor comments" above). The authors state that "checkpoints" will be publicly available but do not mention anything about code release.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper should not be accepted due limitations of the methods in terms of efficiency and applicability (weakness 1 and 3). Also, the empirical evidence provided is not convincing (weakness 2 and 4).

It is similar to FROST, which uses the model to first generate an entity chain, followed by a summary based on that entity chain. The authors continue to pretrain the PEGASUS summarization model to generate entity chains and summaries with pseudo-labels. The LM parameters are frozen during finetuning, and only the Prefix part is learned.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a two-stage approach for abstractive summarization with controlled entity chains. The authors first pretrain the model with soft prompts on the C4 dataset to predict entity chains and the pseudo summary. Then the authors fine-tune the model to generate the entity chains and the summary. Experiments shows a certain level of effectiveness of some of the included techniques.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strength**

This paper discusses a possible solution to include soft prompt and entity chains for controllable summarization

**Weakness** 

There are certain levels concerns from the following aspects:

**Novelty**: this paper seems to be a mixture of existing techniques. Tuning soft prompts is proposed and discussed in Li and Liang 2021 and Lester et. al. 2021. Using entities for improving and controlling summarization is previously discussed in many works, for example Sharma et. al. 2019. Combining these techniques seems to be more of an engineering effort than scientific contribution. 

**Issues on efficiency**: the authors claim that their approach is parameter and data efficient. Yet this paper uses C4 to pretrain the language model, which is neither parameter nor data efficient. Although the following fine-tune stage only tunes the prompt, it would be improper to turn a blind eye on the pretraining stage. 

**Comparison with PEGASUS**: as this paper starts from a pretrained PEGASUS model, a natural choice is to view PEGASUS as a primary baseline. I may have missed something here, yet it seems that after the proposed pretraining and fine-tuning stages, the resulting model does not outperform the PEGASUS model at all (Table 2), which makes one to question the effectiveness of the proposed methods. 

**Experiment setup:** there is also unclarities about the experimental setup. Basically, a rule of thumb here is **only change one factor** while **keeping the rest of the factors the same**. For example:

- If the authors would like to demonstrate the overall approach, then a reasonable setting would be: keeping the backbone model the same, the number of data the same (pretained data also count), compare the two-stage approach in this paper with standard fine-tuning.
- If the authors would like to demonstrate parameter efficiency, then a reasonable setting would be: keeping the backbone model the same, the number of tunable parameters the same (so cannot pretrain because it changes all the model parameter), the number of data the same (pertrained data also count), then compare two different parameter-efficiency methods (for example, comparing with LoRA)

Yet in Table 2, it would be very hard to compare models due to multiple changing factors: the number of tunable parameters are not the same; the base model is not the same; this work has additional pretraining while others may not; this work uses explicit entity models while others  have not. Given these facts, unless I have missed something, it would be very hard to conclude that this work is truly parameter-efficient or data-efficient. 

**Reference**

Li and Liang 2021. Prefix-Tuning: Optimizing Continuous Prompts for Generation

Lester et. al. 2021. The Power of Scale for Parameter-Efficient Prompt Tuning

Sharma et. al. 2019. An Entity-Driven Framework for Abstractive Summarization
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
**Clarity:** Table 4 is very hard to parse. I can make an educated guess yet feel like refrained to do so. It would be great if the authors could clearly state what are the differences between models (e.g., what are the differences between Soft PT v.s. PromptSum?). Also a suggestion is that, when doing ablation study, a good practice is to gradually remove the component, one at a time, to see each component’s effect.  

**Novelty**: as mentioned above, this paper seems to be a mixture of existing techniques. Tuning soft prompts is proposed and discussed in Li and Liang 2021 and Lester et. al. 2021. Using entities for improving and controlling summarization is previously discussed in many works, for example Sharma et. al. 2019. Combining these techniques seems to be more of an engineering effort than scientific contribution.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper proposes a two-stage approach for abstractive summarization with controlled entity chains. The idea of using entity chains to control summarization is valid and inspiring. Yet the major problem is that the experiments is conducted in a way that multiple factors are simultaneously changing, such that it is very hard to verify the proposed methods are effective. Also this paper starts from a pretrained PEGASUS checkpoint, yet the resulting model seems not outperforming PEGASUS. I would suggest the authors to redesign the experiments to show more clear comparison, and explicitly state what is being controlled and what is being compared.

content.title: PromptSum: Planning with Mixed Prompts for Parameter-Efficient Controllable Abstractive Summarization
content.abstract: Prompt tuning (PT), a technique that only tunes the additional prompt embeddings while keeping the backbone pretrained language model frozen, has shown promising results in language understanding tasks, especially in low-resource scenarios. However, there lacks better prompt design methods for generation tasks such as summarization. At the same time, summarization guided through instructions (discrete prompts) can achieve a desirable double objective of higher quality and controllability in summary generation. Towards a triple goal of data-efficiency, parameter-efficiency and controllability, we introduce PromptSum, a method combining PT with a multi-task objective and discrete entity prompts for abstractive summarization. Our model achieves state-of-the-art results on several popular few-shot benchmarks as well as a strong level of controllability through entities, all while only tuning several orders of magnitude less parameters.
